In response to climate and resource challenges, the transition to a renewable and
decentralized energy system is imperative. Ultrathin Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS)-based
solar cells are compatible with such transition due to their low material usage and
improved production throughput. Despite the benchmark efﬁciency of CIGS
technology, ultrathin conﬁgurations face efﬁciency drops arising from increased rear
interface recombination and incomplete light absorption. Dielectric passivation
schemes address rear interface recombination, but achieving simultaneous electrical
and optical gains is crucial for thinning down the absorber. Plasmonic nanoparticles
emerge as a solution, enhancing light interaction through resonant scattering. In the
proposed architecture, the nanoparticles are encapsulated within a dielectric rear
passivation layer, combining effective passivation and light trapping. A controlled
deposition and encapsulation of individualized nanoparticles is achieved by an
optimized process ﬂow using microﬂuidic devices and nanoimprint lithography.

circuit current density and a 23 mV open-circuit voltage improvements are obtained,

tackle the electrical and optical downfalls arising from the absorber thickness
reduction, contributing to the dissemination of ultrathin technology.

1) increased rear interface recombination and 2) incomplete light
absorption.[10,16,17,19–21] To address the rear interface recombina-
tion, passivation schemes based on patterned dielectric layers,
such as SiO2,[20,22–25] Al2O3,[26–30] HfO2,[31,32] and TiO2,[33,34]
have been efﬁciently introduced, yielding promising enhance-
ments in open-circuit voltage (VOC), with improvements over
100 mV compared with a nonpassivated device.[20] However, to
tackle the challenges imposed through the absorber thickness
reduction, the electrical gains provided by dielectric passivation
contact schemes need to be coupled with signiﬁcant optical
gains, as thinning down the absorber from 2000 to 500 nm
leads to losses in the short-circuit current density (JSC) that
can be as high as 4 mA cm2.[17] The dielectric rear interface pas-
sivation architectures already allow for a rear optical reﬂectance
improvement, usually around 0.1–0.9 mA cm2,[20,22,35,36] due to
a refractive index mismatch between the absorber and the dielec-
tric layer with a low refractive index.[19,36] Nevertheless, consid-
ering a CIGS-based absorber with a bandgap energy value of
1.16 eV and assuming an ideal charge carrier collection, even
if a perfect metallic mirror is integrated at the rear of an ultrathin
device with a 500 nm absorber, the simulated JSC value is still
2 mA cm2 lower than the one of the conventional architecture
with a 2 μm absorber.[17] Hence, besides an increased optical rear
reﬂection with the passivation layer, incorporated scattering strat-
egies to further improve light absorption remain a crucial aspect
to attain high-performance ultrathin solar cells. Plasmonic nano-
particles (NPs) have emerged as a compelling solution, having
been integrated into several solar cell technologies.[37–40] The
NPs can signiﬁcantly enhance light interaction through plas-
monic resonance effects, which involve the collective oscillation
of free electrons within the NP when exposed to speciﬁc light
wavelengths, which may lead to both far-ﬁeld scattering and
near-ﬁeld localization, increasing the chances of photon absorp-
tion within the absorber.[21,41,42] Regarding the placement of
metallic NPs within an ultrathin CIGS-based solar cell architec-
ture, there are reports of these being placed at either the solar cell
front surface or at the p–n junction[43–45] or integrated within the
rear contact architecture.[46,47] However, if the NPs are placed
above the absorber, those would block a portion of the incident
light,
through
reﬂectance
or
parasitic
absorbance.[17,21]
Therefore, a more beneﬁcial approach involves placing NPs at
the absorber rear.[17,21,48] In this conﬁguration, the NPs will inter-
act with long-wavelength light not absorbed during the initial tra-
versal through the solar cell, thereby minimizing undesirable
parasitic optical losses.[49] At resonant wavelength values, the
NPs may scatter or absorb the incoming light; thus, the absorbed
light in the metallic NPs will not lead to photocurrent generation.
Hence, the plasmonic architecture should be optimized for an
optical path length enhancement by maximizing the scattering
efﬁciency rather than the absorption one. However, the integra-
tion at the absorber rear requires the encapsulation of the metal-
lic NPs, as the CIGS-based layer deposition temperatures between
300 and 600 °C could lead to in-diffusion.[17,21,50–52] Thus, some
architectural solutions have been proposed, such as integration
within a transparent conductive oxide (TCO),[47] albeit without
the demonstration of solar cell devices, or even the use of ther-
mally stable Mo NPs.[46] Nevertheless, encapsulating the NPs with
a thick TCO dampens the scattering efﬁciency, and using Mo with
weak scattering resonances requires very large NPs that hamper
the
absorber
growth,
leading
to
VOC
value
degradation.
Consequently, an architecture involving the encapsulation of
NPs with a thin dielectric rear passivation layer has been pro-
posed.[17,53,54] In a prior study, the effective encapsulation of
micrometer-sized Au NP aggregates with a 25 nm Al2O3 layer
in a complete CIGS-based device was demonstrated through
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy depth analysis.[54] The integration
of these metallic aggregates resulted in an optical enhancement.
However, the developed Au aggregates, being micrometer sized,
created a highly irregular and rough rear interface, which contrib-
uted to a decrease in the VOC and conversion efﬁciency values in
comparison to a reference device.[54] Thus, in this work, a combi-
nation of a controlled procedure using a microﬂuidic device to
deposit individualized 105 nm Au NPs with a nanoimprint lithog-
raphy (NIL) approach to create electrical contacts was developed.
Therefore, a substrate that combines passivation through the
dielectric scheme while allowing for the utilization of the substan-
tial passivation area (> 70%) for effective light trapping through
individual metallic NPs was achieved. The proposed architecture
allows to have NPs close to the solar cell absorber, effectively
exploiting the plasmonic scattering of small NPs that do not ham-
per the absorber layer growth and degrade the device performance.
The developed plasmonic and passivated architecture allowed for a
3.7 mA cm2 JSC increase over a nonpassivated reference device, as
well as a 23 mV VOC improvement. The combined passivation and
optical improvement from the novel architecture led to an almost
2% absolute light-to-power conversion efﬁciency enhancement in
comparison to a nonpassivated reference device. The attained
results show the potential to couple optical with electrical strategies
through the exploitation of plasmonic NPs encapsulated by a
dielectric passivation scheme in ultrathin solar cells.

tecture considerations were followed to achieve an effective solar
cell substrate in which both passivation and light-trapping capa-
bilities
can
be
optimized.
Regarding
the
passivating
material, Al2O3 was chosen as it has been previously used for
an effective passivation of active recombination mechanisms
at the rear interface,[26,27] as well as exploited as a barrier layer
for metals in ultrathin solar cells,[47,54–56] enabling the metallic
NPs integration. With respect to the contacting approach, a
high-passivating area is desired for a more substantial decrease
in the active recombination mechanisms, while allowing for the
utilization of the signiﬁcant passivation area for effective light
trapping through the encapsulation of metallic NPs.[20,23,57]
Nevertheless, the high passivation area needs to be counterbal-
anced with a contacting area which does not compromise the
charge extraction, as passivation areas higher than 90% have
shown an impact on ultrathin solar cells’ series resistance.[9,20,23]
Therefore, in this work, a line contact pattern with a nominal
passivation area of 75% was chosen to attain an effective passiv-
ation and allow a substantial dielectric coverage to couple with
light trapping, without hindering charge carrier collection.
The dielectric encapsulation layer thickness is as well critical,
since the encapsulation of the metallic nanostructures needs
to be ensured. However, the thickness of the dielectric layer
might have an impact in the resonant behavior of the metallic
NPs. The charge polarization in the NP through an external elec-
tromagnetic ﬁeld will induce a charge accumulation with the
opposite sign at the metallic NP/dielectric medium interface,
which will in turn screen the induced electric ﬁeld in the
NP.[58] The screening effect is dependent on the polarizability
of the dielectric medium, with a higher-refractive-index medium
leading to a redshift of the plasmonic resonance peak and a
stronger resonant intensity.[58,59] Therefore, the thickness of
the dielectric layer will have a signiﬁcant impact on the plas-
monic resonance as it will lower the medium’s local refractive
index at the NPs vicinity and suppress the resonant scatter-
ing.[48,60] A 25 nm Al2O3 layer has been previously used to effec-
tively encapsulate micrometer-large Au NPs aggregates.[54]
Nevertheless, to dampen the unwanted effects on the NPs’ scat-
tering efﬁciency and considering that individual NPs will be
encapsulated herein in comparison to micrometer-large NPs
aggregates, the encapsulation layer thickness value used was
of 15 nm. Regarding the plasmonic material, Au was chosen
due to the ease of achieving a NPs colloidal solution, high
free-electron density, and stability.[61–63] Furthermore, there is
a size dependence for the absorption and scattering cross section
of the NPs. Thus, the diameter of the used NPs is critical in hav-
ing an efﬁcient scattering substrate. For the selection of the NPs
diameter, the absorption (σabs) and scattering cross sections
(σscat) of Au NPs with diameters ranging between 40 and
140 nm, within a CIGS-based medium, were simulated through
the ﬁnite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method using the
Lumerical software.[64] The NPs were capped by a 15 nm
Al2O3 shell in these simulations, which was the chosen encap-
sulation thickness value within the passivation line contact
scheme. In Figure 1a the normalized scattering cross-section
(Qscat = σscat/G, with G being the geometric cross-section) spec-
tra of the simulated NPs with different diameters are shown. The
Qscat is lowest through the whole wavelength range for a NP
diameter value of 40 nm. Through the diameter value increase
to 60 nm, there is a sharp enhancement of the Qscat maximum
peak along with a redshift. For diameter values below 80 nm, the
NPs only sustain a dipolar resonant mode, presenting a sharp
resonant peak in the Qscat spectra. As the NPs diameter increases
above 60 nm, the dipolar peak at longer wavelength values
redshifts and higher-order resonant modes appear, leading to
a broadening and dampening of the Qscat.[37,58] In Figure 1b,
a plot evaluating the NPs’ scattering efﬁciency over wavelength
is shown.[37] For the smallest studied size, the scattering efﬁ-
ciency is below 50%, meaning that for these small NPs, the
absorption is dominating the normalized extinction cross section

For an effective integration of the metallic NPs within the
ultrathin solar cell, it is essential to completely etch the dielectric
matrix with Au NPs in the desired regions to create line contacts.
If residual Au is left in the line contacts, it may diffuse during the
high-temperature deposition, hampering the solar cell perfor-

a C4F8-based chemistry was used, which allowed to obtain a
well-deﬁned line pattern without Au NPs in the contacts, as
shown in the SEM image of the patterned substrate in
Figure 7a. Nevertheless, the line pattern may etch through the
NPs, exposing a minor quantity of Au, which could negatively
impact the VOC. An atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis
was conducted, as presented in Figure 7b, for an accurate mea-
surement of the pattern dimensions. The averaged measured
line width was of 660 nm with a pitch value of 2810 nm, very
close to the nominal desired values, resulting in a passivation
area of 77%. In addition, an overetch of 11 nm was measured,
assuring a complete etch of the Al2O3/Au NPs/Al2O3 stack.
An ultrathin ACIGS layer with a ﬂat [Ga]/([Ga]þ[In]) proﬁle
was deposited on top of the passivated plasmonic substrate
(PPS), as well as in a reference SLG/Mo substrate (Ref ) at a
growth temperature of 550 °C. The absorber deposition was
followed by chemical bath deposition of CdS and sputtering of
the window i-ZnO/Al:ZnO bilayer.[50] SEM cross-section images
of both prepared devices, Ref and PPS, prior to the window
deposition are shown in Figure 8a,b, respectively. The ACIGS
layer appears to be uniform for both devices, with large grains
and without any clear shunting paths, meaning that the presence
of the Au NPs did not affect the ACIGS layer growth. An absorber
thickness of 450 nm was obtained for both devices. The SEM
analysis suggests an effective encapsulation of the Au NPs with
the thin dielectric layer in the PPS device, with the NPs remain-
ing with a spherical shape even after the harsh ACIGS layer depo-
sition, that is, a 550 °C temperature and Se atmosphere. The NPs
remain intact and encapsulated after the absorber deposition,
which shows the viability of using a passivation layer for the
NPs encapsulation, enabling the exploitation of the resonant
scattering effects.

4. Experimental Section
Nanoparticles Solution Preparation: The synthesis of Au NP seeds
followed the Turkevitch method.[71] A 200.5 mL aqueous solution of chlor-
oauric acid (HAuCl4) with a 0.25 mM concentration was heated to its boil-
ing point. Upon boiling, a 20.1 mL solution of a previously warmed 40 mM
sodium citrate tribasic dihydrate was quickly added. The entire process
involved continuous heating and magnetic stirring. Instantly, the solution
became transparent, and in a period between 15 to 20 min, it gradually
transformed into a red wine color, indicating completion. The Au NP seeds
were subsequently grown using a hydroxylamine seeding method.[67]
A solution was prepared by combining 0.67 mL of an 80 mM aqueous
hydroxylamine–hydrochloride solution with 60.15 mL of an aqueous
0.25 mM HAuCl4 solution. After 15 min of magnetic stirring, 0.38 mL of
seed solution was added to grow the NPs to the nominal target between
100 and 120 nm. The solution was kept under constant stirring until a
cloudy brown color was achieved. The grown Au NPs were stabilized
by adding 0.9 mL of a 40 mM aqueous sodium citrate solution. The
NPs were washed through centrifugation at 3500 rpm for 15 min and
redispersed in milli-q water.
PDMS Device Preparation: To produce microﬂuidic devices, the
development of a Si device master mold was ﬁrst required. The device
was designed to ensure a uniform solution injection and avoid bubble
formation, by implementing multiple uniformly spaced microﬂuidic chan-
nels, as shown in Figure 11.
For the master mold, a Si wafer was coated with 2.2 μm-thick AZ P4110
resist coating through spin coating in a Karl Suss Optical Track system.
Afterward, the device design was imprinted onto the coated Si wafer using
a Heidelberg DWL 2000. Subsequently, the regions exposed to the design
underwent development with AZ400K. To etch the Si wafer into the desired
structure, a RIE process using a SF6 and C4F8 plasma chemistry with a
SPTS Pegasus system was performed. For the device production, a mixture
of PDMS and a crosslinker, Sylgard 184 elastomer curing agent, was pre-
pared in a 10:1 ratio, resulting in a uniform gel. The PDMS gel was then
poured into the Si master mold. To ensure consistent gel coverage, the Si
master mold and PDMS system were subjected to a vacuum environment
within a desiccator. The Si master mold and PDMS assembly underwent
curing at 65 °C for 2 h, following which the device was separated from the
Si master mold.

reﬂectance and scattering, as well as, an improved charge carrier
collection and rear surface recombination velocity value decrease,
shown through optical and electrical simulations. Overall,
an almost 2% light-to-power conversion efﬁciency value enhance-
ment was obtained for the developed plasmonic and
passivated architecture.
4. Experimental Section
Nanoparticles Solution Preparation: The synthesis of Au NP seeds
followed the Turkevitch method.[71] A 200.5 mL aqueous solution of chlor-
oauric acid (HAuCl4) with a 0.25 mM concentration was heated to its boil-
ing point. Upon boiling, a 20.1 mL solution of a previously warmed 40 mM
sodium citrate tribasic dihydrate was quickly added. The entire process
involved continuous heating and magnetic stirring. Instantly, the solution
became transparent, and in a period between 15 to 20 min, it gradually
transformed into a red wine color, indicating completion. The Au NP seeds
were subsequently grown using a hydroxylamine seeding method.[67]
A solution was prepared by combining 0.67 mL of an 80 mM aqueous
hydroxylamine–hydrochloride solution with 60.15 mL of an aqueous
0.25 mM HAuCl4 solution. After 15 min of magnetic stirring, 0.38 mL of
seed solution was added to grow the NPs to the nominal target between
100 and 120 nm. The solution was kept under constant stirring until a
cloudy brown color was achieved. The grown Au NPs were stabilized
by adding 0.9 mL of a 40 mM aqueous sodium citrate solution. The
NPs were washed through centrifugation at 3500 rpm for 15 min and
redispersed in milli-q water.
PDMS Device Preparation: To produce microﬂuidic devices, the
development of a Si device master mold was ﬁrst required. The device
was designed to ensure a uniform solution injection and avoid bubble
formation, by implementing multiple uniformly spaced microﬂuidic chan-
nels, as shown in Figure 11.
For the master mold, a Si wafer was coated with 2.2 μm-thick AZ P4110
resist coating through spin coating in a Karl Suss Optical Track system.
Afterward, the device design was imprinted onto the coated Si wafer using
a Heidelberg DWL 2000. Subsequently, the regions exposed to the design
underwent development with AZ400K. To etch the Si wafer into the desired
structure, a RIE process using a SF6 and C4F8 plasma chemistry with a
SPTS Pegasus system was performed. For the device production, a mixture
of PDMS and a crosslinker, Sylgard 184 elastomer curing agent, was pre-
pared in a 10:1 ratio, resulting in a uniform gel. The PDMS gel was then
poured into the Si master mold. To ensure consistent gel coverage, the Si
master mold and PDMS system were subjected to a vacuum environment
within a desiccator. The Si master mold and PDMS assembly underwent
curing at 65 °C for 2 h, following which the device was separated from the
Si master mold.

Substrate Preparation: The NPs were injected through the PDMS device
channels on a typical SLG/Mo substrate coated with 10 nm of Al2O3. To
prepare for the colloidal solution injection into the device, holes for tube
connections were made. Subsequently, the substrate surface underwent
an O2 plasma treatment to enhance adhesion at the interface when it
bonded to the PDMS device. Afterward, the PDMS device was attached
to the substrate and subjected to 20 min of heating at 65 °C. The ﬁnal step
consisted of injecting the NPs solution into the microﬂuidic device using a
syringe through microtubes. Following an optimized drying period, the
PDMS device was separated from the substrate. The Au NPs were then
encapsulated with Al2O3. For the Al2O3 layers deposition the ALD Beneq
TFS 200 system was employed at 200 °C, involving 143 cycles of trimethy-
laluminium (TMA) and DI water, with pulse/purge step durations of 150/
650 ms (TMA) and 150/1000 ms (water). For the contact scheme pattern-
ing, NIL was utilized. The developed pattern consisted of trenches with a
nominal width of 700 nm and a nominal pitch of 2800 nm. A hexamethyl-
disilizane (HMDS) vapor priming stage was conducted to enhance pho-
toresist adhesion on the substrate. A 200 nm layer of mr.NIL60002E resist
was spin coated onto the substrate using the Karl Suss Optical Track sys-
tem. The trench pattern was subsequently imprinted onto the substrate
through NIL. Initially, the temperature was raised to 65 °C for 10 s, fol-
lowed by increasing the pressure to 15 bar for 100 s. UV light exposure
for 180 s (5500 mJ cm2) was initiated. An O2 strip process to remove
residual resist was conducted using the SPTS Pegasus system, with an O2
ﬂow rate of 115 sccm at 13.56 MHz. RIE process was then performed
using the STPS APS tool with a He, H2, and C4F8 plasma chemistry.
Finally, the unexposed resist was removed using a PVA TEPLA plasma
asher. Besides the prepared PPS with the structure SLG/Mo/Al2O3/Au
NPs/Al2O3, a reference (Ref) one (SLG/Mo) was also used for device
comparison purposes.
Solar Cell Development: In both the Ref and PPS substrates, a 15 nm
layer of sodium ﬂuoride (NaF) was evaporated on top of the complete
prepared substrates. In the same batch, an ultrathin ACIGS layer with
an average thickness of 450 nm, determined through SEM cross-section
analysis, was coevaporated onto both substrates. Elemental composition
analysis using X-ray ﬂuorescence with the Panalytical Epsilon 5 equipment
yielded:
[Cu]/([Ga]þ[In]) = 0.83,
[Ga]/([Ga]þ[In]) = 0.29,
and
[Ag]/
([Ag]þ[Cu]) = 0.11. Further details regarding the ACIGS deposition pro-
cess can be found in other studies.[102–105] The subsequent deposition
of the remaining layers (CdS/i-ZnO/ZnO:Al) followed the standard base-
line as reported elsewhere.[50] A chemical etching method was employed
to pattern individual 0.1 cm2 solar cells in a 1.5  1.5 cm2 square array.[106]
Characterization: TEM employing the JEM-2100-HT instrument was
used to analyze the synthesized Au NPs, with their size determined using
ImageJ software. For the TEM, solutions were deposited onto a carbon
substrate supported by a Cu mesh grid. Relative absorbance and diffuse
reﬂectance measurements were conducted via a Perkin-Elmer Lambda
950
ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared
spectrophotometer.
An
integrat
ing sphere was used for the diffuse reﬂectance measurements. A
FeiNovaNanoSEM 650 high-resolution SEM operating at 5 kV was
employed. A morphological assessment of the patterned sample was per-
formed utilizing the AFM Dimension Icon system. Tapping mode was
used with a scan rate of 0.5 Hz. Illuminated and dark J–V measurements
under AM1.5 G conditions were carried out using an in-house measure-
ment system. The J–V measurements were conducted after a 20 min
period of light exposure. EQE measurements were performed using a
QEX10 equipment, employing a chopped monochromatic light scan
covering wavelengths from 300 to 1100 nm, with a step interval of 5 nm.
Optoelectronic Simulations: For simulating the scattering and absorp-
tion cross sections of the Au NPs, the FDTD numerical method, which
is accessible within the Lumerical software, was used.[64,107] The simula-
tion setup incorporated a total-ﬁeld-scattered-ﬁeld (TFSF) source with a
bandwidth spanning from 300 to 1100 nm. The choice of a TFSF source
allows the decoupling of the scattering behavior of the simulated Au NPs,
as it effectively separates the scattered ﬁeld from the incident ﬁeld. The
optical performance of the developed novel CIGS solar cells was simulated
using the FDTD numerical method to comprehensively investigate the
impact of the new architecture on the optical performance of solar cells
with regard to light-trapping effects. Simulations were performed using a
random polarized broadband plane wave light source. To ensure compu-
tational efﬁciency without compromising accuracy, the smallest mesh size
feasible while meeting time-memory requirements was employed. Critical
interfaces were resolved with a 1 nm mesh size. The Violas et al. ultrathin
solar cell baseline[14,20] was employed to estimate the effect of the
improved charge carrier’s collection through the passivation layer integra-
tion on the JSC value. The optical constants for the several materials used
within this work were obtained from previously reported results.[108–111]
